protein_comment: The subunit structure of this enzyme from Pseudomonas nitroreducens (previously known as Pseudomonas sp. strain HBP1) has not been reported. The gene encoding it has not been isolated. An extradiol ring cleavage dioxygenase activity was partially purified and shown to cleave both catechol and pyrogallol substrates in the meta position [ Kohler93 ].

Catechol 2,3-dioxygenase is an extradiol type dioxygenase that catalyzes the conversion of catechol to (2Z,4E)-2-hydroxy-6-oxohexa-2,4-dienoate with the insertion of two atoms of molecular oxygen. The enzyme from Pseudomonas putida mt-2 has been purified to homogeneity [ Nakai83 ]. The enzyme, which is a homotetramer, contains 1 atom of iron per monomer. Activity ranges betweent 110 to 300 μmol/min/mg protein, depending on iron concentration. The enzyme is very sensitive to oxygen [ Nakai83 ]. The xylE gene encoding the enzyme has been cloned and sequenced [ Nakai83a ].

Alcaligenes sp. O-1 can utilize several sulfonated aromatic compounds, including 4-toluenesulfonate and benzenesulfonate , as sole sources of carbon and energy. For more information, please see 4-toluenesulfonate degradation II and benzenesulfonate degradation . The intermediates in the degradation of these compounds, 4-methylcatechol and catechol , are degraded to TCA cycle intermediates by the meta cleavage pathway of aromatic compounds . The first enzyme in this pathway, responsible for cleaving the aromtic ring, is catechol 2,3-dioxygenase .

2-hydroxymuconic semialdehyde hydrolase catalyzes a rare reaction: the hydrolytic cleavage of a carbon-carbon bond. The enzyme is a serine hydrolase of the αβ family of enzymes. It contains both a serine and a histidine in its active site. The enzyme accepts the ring-cleavage products of both catechol and 3-methylcatechol ( (2Z,4E)-2-hydroxy-6-oxohexa-2,4-dienoate and (2Z,4E)-2-hydroxy-6-oxohepta-2,4-dienoate , respectively) as substrates. K M for the later is lower, at 13.6 μM (vs. 85 μM for the former) [ Diaz95 ].

2-hydroxypentadienoate hydratase (MhpD) converts 2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate (HPD) into 4-hydroxy-2-ketopentanoate [ Pollard98a , Ferrandez97 ]. E. coli is able to utilize certain aromatic acids as carbon and energy sources. A meta-cleavage pathway involving MhpD is used for the catabolism of 3-(3-hydroxyphenyl)propionate [ Burlingame83 ].

The subunit structure of this enzyme has not been reported. This enzyme from Bordetella sp. 10d catalyzes the hydration of (3E)-2-oxopent-3-enoate to form ( S )-4-hydroxy-2-oxopentanoate . This hydratase from Bordetella sp. 10d appears to form a high molecular weight complex with 2-oxo-3-hexenedioate decarboxylase . The complex apparent molecular mass was 470 kDa as determined by gel filtration chromatography. The two enzymes co-purified and resolved to bands of 29 kDa and 27 kDa on SDS-PAGE. The molar ratio of the two enzymes in the complex was 1:1 [ Orii06 ]. Similar complexes between these two enzymes have been found in other species (see 2-oxo-3-hexenedioate decarboxylase (AmnE) and 2-oxo-3-hexenedioate decarboxylase (XylI)). The amino-terminal amino acid sequences of the 29 kDa and 27 kDa bands were distinct and analysis identified them as the decarboxylase and hydratase, respectively [ Orii06 ].

The cnbE and cnbF genes of Comamonas testosteroni CNB-1 were cloned and expressed simultaneously together in Escherichia coli . The recombinant host was able to convert (3Z)-2-chloro-5-oxohex-3-enedioate to 5-chloro-4-hydroxy-2-oxopentanoate [ Wu06 ]. Neither of these two proteins has been purified.
A plasmid expressing the todFC1C2BADEG gene cluster of Pseudomonas putida F1 in Escherichia coli accumulated ( S )-4-hydroxy-2-oxopentanoate [ Lau94 ].

Expression of a plasmid containing the Ralstonia pickettii (strain PKO1) toluene degradation gene cluster in a Pseudomonas aeruginosa mutant allowed it to grow on toluene, or related compounds, as a sole carbon source. The activities of the enzymes involved were assayed using unpurified proteins in cell extracts [ Kukor91 ]. At the time the substrate of the enzyme was believed to be 2-oxopent-4-enoate (it is now known that the actual substrate is its tautomer (2Z)-2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate ). 2-oxopent-4-enoate was prepared by processing (2S)-2-amino-4-pentenoate with EC 1.4.3.2, L -amino-acid oxidase , as previosuly described by [ Collinsworth73 ]. Hydratase activity with with 2-oxopent-4-enoate was observed in the cell extracts. By subcloning different sections of the gene cluster into Pseudomonas aeruginosa the activity could be associated with the tbuJ gene, which is located in the furthest position from the cluster's promoter [ Kukor91 ]. In the pathway for toluene degradation proposed by the authors the enzyme was proposed to act on the alternative substrate (2Z)-2-hydroxyhexa-2,5-dienoate [ Kukor91 ]. While this proposal seems plausible, this specific activity has not been demonstrated by a direct assay.
2-Hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate hydratase catalyzes the ninth reaction in p -cymene degradation [ Eaton96 ].

2-oxopent-4-enoate hydratase from Pseudomonas putida mt-2 forms a complex with 2-oxo-3-hexenedioate decarboxylase that converts (3 E )-2-oxohex-3-enedioate to ( S )-4-hydroxy-2-oxopentanoate via the intermediate (2Z)-2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate (although previous work suggested that the intermediate is (2E)-2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate [ Stanley00 ]).

4-hydroxy-2-ketopentanoate aldolase (MhpE) is a stereospecific class I aldolase [ Pollard98 ]. The expression of MhpE is translationally coupled to MhpF, and interaction between the two proteins appears to be required for solubility of MhpE [ Lee06a ]. E. coli is able to utilize certain aromatic acids as carbon and energy sources. A meta-cleavage pathway involving MhpE is used for the catabolism of 3-phenylpropionate [ Burlingame83 ]. MhpE: " m - h ydroxyphenyl p ropionate"

The final two steps of the meta -cleavage pathway in Pseudomonas sp. CF600 involve the conversion of ( S )-4-hydroxy-2-oxopentanoate to pyruvate and acetyl-CoA by the enzymes 4-hydroxy-2-oxovalerate aldolase and acetaldehyde dehydrogenase (acylating) . Biochemical studies demonstrated that these two enzymes comprise a bifunctional aldolase-dehydrogenase heterodimer, and suggest that the product of the aldolase reaction, acetaldehyde , is transferred to the dehydrogenase active site via a channeling mechanism. This minimizes the risk to the cells posed by the toxic acetaldehyde . The reaction is stimulated by Mn 2+ and by NADH , and, to a lesser extent, NAD + [ Powlowski93 ].
4-Hydroxy-2-oxovalerate aldolase catalyzes the tenth reaction in p-cymene degradation [ Eaton96 ].

The predicted amino acid sequence of the todH gene product showed very high identity with other bacterial 4-hydroxy-2-oxovalerate aldolase gene products. The presence of the todH gene product in Pseudomonas putida F1 was suggested by the protein expression pattern of plasmid constructs [ Lau94 ]. The subunit composition of this enzyme has not been determined.

Expression of a plasmid containing the Ralstonia pickettii (strain PKO1) toluene degradation gene cluster in a Pseudomonas aeruginosa mutant allowed it to grow on toluene, or related compounds, as a sole carbon source. The activities of the enzymes involved were assayed using unpurified proteins in cell extracts [ Kukor91 ]. The activity of this enzyme was determined indirectly from pyruvate production by measuring the rate of oxidation of NADH in the presence of excess lactate dehydrogenase. The substrate for the assay was ( S )-4-hydroxy-2-oxopentanoate , which was prepared by mild alkaline hydrolysis of 4-methyl-2-oxobutyrolactone [ Kukor91 ]. In the pathway for toluene degradation proposed by the authors the enzyme was proposed to act on the alternative substrate ( S )-4-hydroxy-2-oxohexanoate [ Kukor91 ]. While this proposal seems plausible, this specific activity has not been demonstrated by a direct assay.

In Pseudomonas putida , the TOL plasmid pWW0 encodes all the enzymes responsible for the degradation of toluene and xylene. The genes encoding these enzymes are organized into two operons: the upper operon, which contains the three enzymes involved in the upper pathway, and the meta operon, which contains the genes responsible for the degradation of benzoates and toluates via the lower pathway. The xylK gene catalyzes the penultimate step in the pathway, the retro-aldol cleavage of 4-hydroxy-2-oxopentanoate to pyruvate and acetaldehyde. It has been established already in 1981 that only xylJ and xylK are required for growth on (2S)-2-amino-4-pentenoate [ Kunz81 ]. Original publications that characterized the genes encoding the meta operon ( xyKYZLEGFJIH ) missed the xylK gene [ Harayama84 , Harayama86 ]. Genetic characterization of transposon mutants unable to grow on (2S)-2-amino-4-pentenoate identified the location of the gene between xylJ and xylI [ Harayama89a ]. In a subsequent study all of the meta -cleavage genes were cloned into an expression vector and expressed in Escherichia coli maxicells, showing that xylK encodes a 4-hydroxy-2-oxovalerate aldolase [ Harayama90 ].
Heterologous expression of EutE in various yeasts increases the level of acetylating acetaldehyde dehydrogenase activity in the cells and has been used in metabolic engineering [ Kozak14 , Song16a ].

mhpF encodes an acetylating acetaldehyde dehydrogenase [ Ferrandez97 ]. MhpF is active as a monomer; the rate-limiting step of the reaction appears to be transthioesterification [ Fischer13 ]. MhpF is involved in synthesis of n -butanol in an engineered reversal of the β-oxidation pathway [ Dellomonaco11 ]. The expression of MhpE is translationally coupled to MhpF, and interaction between the two proteins appears to be required for solubility of MhpE [ Lee06a ].

native_name: fused acetaldehyde-CoA dehydrogenase and iron-dependent alcohol dehydrogenase

protein_comment: The eutE gene of Salmonella enterica is located in the ethanolamine utilization operon, and encodes a 476-amino-acid protein with 45% similarity (29% identity) to the N-terminal part of the adhE gene of Escherichia coli , which encodes an acetaldehyde dehydrogenase. A Δ eutE mutant was unable to grow on ethanolamine as a sole carbon source, but was able to use it as a nitrogen source [ Penrod06 ].

ADH1 encodes a dual function alcohol dehydrogenase / acetaldehyde dehydrogenase. It appears to be active under anoxic conditions and participates in two different anaerobic ethanol production pathways in Chlamydomonas [ Magneschi12 ].

A CoA-dependent aldehyde dehydrogenase has been partially purified from Leuconostoc mesenteroides . The enzyme could not be separated from an NAD-linked alcohol dehydrogenase that co-purified with it [ Kazahaya72 ]. The enzyme was specific to NAD and could not use NADP. While acetaldehyde and 1-propanal were the best substrates, the enzyme could also use 1-butanal (31% of activity with acetaldehyde) and isobutanal (14%) [ Kazahaya72 ].

The enzyme aldehyde dehydrogenase has not been purified from Syntrophotalea acetylenica . However, the enzymatic activity was measured in crude extracts from acetylene- and acetoin-grown cells. The activity was 0.83 μmol/min/mg protein for acetylene-grown cells, and 0.95 μmol/min/mg protein for acetoin-grown cells [ Schink85 ].

The final two steps of the meta -cleavage pathway in Pseudomonas sp. CF600 involve the conversion of ( S )-4-hydroxy-2-oxopentanoate to pyruvate and acetyl-CoA by the enzymes 4-hydroxy-2-oxovalerate aldolase and acetaldehyde dehydrogenase (acylating) . Biochemical studies demonstrated that these two enzymes comprise a bifunctional aldolase-dehydrogenase heterodimer, and suggest that the product of the aldolase reaction, acetaldehyde , is transferred to the dehydrogenase active site via a channeling mechanism. This minimizes the risk to the cells posed by the toxic acetaldehyde [ Powlowski93 ].

The predicted amino acid sequence of the todI gene product showed very high identity with other bacterial acylating aldehyde dehydrogenase gene products. The presence of the todI gene product in Pseudomonas putida F1 was suggested by the protein expression pattern of plasmid constructs [ Lau94 ]. The subunit composition of this enzyme has not been determined.

The adhE gene of Clostridium acetobutylicum ATCC 824 encodes a multifunctional enzyme that catalyzes both an alcohol dehydrogenase and an acetaldehyde dehydrogenase activities. Both activities are necessary for the formation of butan-1-ol and ethanol during solventogenesis. The adhE gene is part of the sol operon, which is located on the pSOL1 megaplasmid [ Cornillot97 , Nair94a ]. Expression of the gene from a plasmid in Clostridium acetobutylicum ATCC 824 resulted in elevated activities of NADH-dependent butanol dehydrogenase, NAD-dependent acetaldehyde dehydrogenase and butyraldehyde dehydrogenase, and a small increase in NADH-dependent ethanol dehydrogenase [ Nair94a ]. Complementation of a mutant deficient in butyraldehyde dehydrogenase, acetoacetate decarboxylase, and acetoacetyl-coenzyme A:acetate/butyrate:coenzyme A-transferase activities, which produces neither butanol nor acetone, by the adhE gene resulted in restored butanol formation without any acetone formation or any significant increase in ethanol production, suggesting that the primary role of the enzyme is in butanol formation, providing both a butanal dehydrogenase activity (converting butanoyl-CoA to 1-butanal ) and butanol dehydrogenase activity [ Nair94 ]. In addition, inactivation of the gene drastically reduced butanol production (by 85%), supporting this role [ Green96 , Green98 ]. Another gene from the pSOL1 plasmid, adhE2 , encodes a second multifunctional aldehyde/alcohol dehydrogenase involved in butanol production. However, that enzyme is produced only under alcohologenic conditions, and is not expressed under solventogenic conditions [ Fontaine02 ]. Two other NADH-dependent butanol dehydrogenases (BDH I and BDH II) have also been purified, and their genes ( bdhA and bdhB ) have been cloned. The gene from strain ATCC 824 was originally called aad .

A study of Bilophila wadsworthia proteins induced by growth on taurine and isethionate identified two genomic clusters. One of the clusters contained genes encoding a glycyl radical enzyme ( islA ) and its cognate activating enzyme ( islB ), as well as a predicted CoA-acylating aldehyde dehydrogenase ( adhE ) [ Peck19 ]. Since the glycyl radical enzyme ( EC 4.4.1.38, isethionate sulfite-lyase ) produces acetaldehyde , it was proposed that AdhE may convert it to acetyl-CoA . The gene was cloned with a His-tag and expressed in Escherichia coli , and the recombinant protein was purified. The purified enzyme was incubated with coenzyme A , NAD+ or NADP+, and acetaldehyde . No reaction was observed when the reaction was run at pH 7.5, but formation of acetyl-CoA was observed at a pH of 8. The enzyme preferred NAD+ over NADP [ Peck19 ].
